summary: 5a resolves Reish Lakish's challenge to R. Yochanan (from the preceding discussion): if we derive YK from the inauguration, all inauguration requirements should invalidate the YK service. Four Amoraim name practical differences between R. Yochanan (who holds that all inauguration requirements invalidate) and R. Chanina (who holds only those that would invalidate ongoing service also invalidate the inauguration). Rav Yosef names semikha (laying hands on the offering); Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak names tenufah (waving); Rav Pappa names prisha (seven-day sequestering). In the second sugya, Ravina adds rivui shiva (wearing multiple garments for seven days) and meshicha shiva (anointing for seven days). The Gemara then provides sources from Lev. 16:32 for why any combination of anointing and garment-wearing over seven days suffices. R. Yitzchak bar Bisna identifies the word 'kachah' (thus/so) as the source for R. Yochanan's invalidation principle, and the daf's own text cuts off mid-sentence immediately after affirming this works for what is explicitly written ('tinach kol milta'); per Rashi's note on the final word, the anticipated continuation on the next page asks about requirements written elsewhere in the Torah.

display.title: R. Yochanan vs. R. Chanina: semikha, tenufah, and prisha as practical differences
display.oneLine: Three authorities list practical differences between R. Yochanan (all inauguration requirements invalidate) and R. Chanina (only those that invalidate ongoing service invalidate the inauguration): semikha, tenufah, and prisha each do not invalidate ongoing service and thus diverge.
display.shortSummary: Rav Yosef identifies semikha (laying hands on the offering) as a point of divergence: R. Yochanan would say failure to perform semikha at the inauguration invalidates, while R. Chanina says it does not, because semikha does not invalidate ongoing service. A baraita proves semikha does not invalidate ongoing service: Lev. 1:4 says laying hands causes the offering 'to be accepted' - but does waving hands atone? No, only blood atones. The verse must be teaching that if you treat semikha as optional (a 'shirei mitzva'), the Torah credits you as if you did not achieve full atonement - even though you did atone. The same structure applies to tenufah (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak). For prisha, Rav Pappa notes that the mishna uses 'matkin' (designate) not 'mafrishin' (separate), proving the backup priest does not need to be sequestered - which means sequestering does not invalidate ongoing service.
display.whats: The Gemara now resolves Reish Lakish's challenge to R. Yochanan from the preceding discussion. R. Yochanan held that all inauguration requirements invalidate because of the word 'kachah' - do exactly as written. R. Chanina had a narrower principle: only those requirements that would invalidate ordinary ongoing service also invalidate the inauguration. Three authorities name items where these views diverge. Rav Yosef: semikha. At the inauguration, the Kohen laid hands on the offering (a requirement written there). Does failure to do semikha invalidate? R. Yochanan says yes. R. Chanina says no - because semikha does not invalidate ongoing sacrificial service. Proof from Lev. 1:4: 'he shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering and it shall be accepted for him to atone' - does hand-laying atone? Only blood atones (Lev. 17:11)! So why say 'to atone'? Because if a person omits semikha, treating it as a secondary mitzva (shirei mitzva), the Torah considers it as if he did not achieve the ideal atonement, even though he still atones. This proves semikha is a shirei mitzva, not indispensable. Tenufah (Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak) follows the same pattern from its verse. Prisha (Rav Pappa): the mishna says 'matkin' (they prepare a backup) not 'mafrishin' (they also separate the backup), showing sequestering is not indispensable for ongoing service.
display.hint: The concept of 'shirei mitzva' (residual mitzva) is key: why does the Torah say 'to atone' in connection with an act that does not actually accomplish atonement? What does this category reveal about how mitzvot work?

learning.learnerQuestion: If semikha doesn't actually atone - only blood atones - why does the verse say 'it shall be accepted for him to atone' when describing semikha?
learning.coreTension: The verse seems to say hand-laying causes atonement. But the Gemara knows from another verse that only blood causes atonement. Something has to give - either the first verse is wrong, or it means something else.
learning.coreMove: Introduce the category of 'shirei mitzva': a residual, secondary component of a mitzva that is not itself the atonement mechanism but whose omission is still counted against you. The verse's 'to atone' is conditional, not causal: it signals that neglecting this optional step means the Torah credits you with less than optimal atonement.
learning.resolution: The verse teaches: if you treat semikha as optional and skip it, the Torah considers this as if your atonement were incomplete - even though you did atone through the blood. This proves semikha is a shirei mitzva (not indispensable), and therefore its omission does not invalidate ongoing service. Consequently (for R. Chanina), it also does not invalidate the inauguration service.

takeaway.text: The category of 'shirei mitzva' captures optional mitzva components: they do not validate or invalidate the core transaction, but their omission still registers as a spiritual deficit. Recognizing this category allows the Gemara to read verses about secondary actions without over-inflating their legal weight.

reasoningPattern.notes: When a verse attributes a function to an act that cannot literally perform that function, the Gemara introduces 'shirei mitzva': the act is secondary and optional, and its omission is scored as incompleteness without being an invalidation.

learning.ahaMoment: The verse says semikha causes 'acceptance' and 'atonement' - but another verse already established that only blood atones. The resolution is not to say one verse overrides the other, but to recognize a different category: optional, residual components of a mitzva that affect how fully you have fulfilled the commandment without being the core mechanism.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may think 'shirei mitzva' means an unimportant mitzva. The Gemara's point is more precise: it is a mitzva that is real and matters spiritually, but is not an invalidation condition. Skipping it doesn't void the service, but it does leave something incomplete.
learning.memoryAnchor: Semikha, tenufah, prisha: three inauguration requirements that don't invalidate ongoing service. The verse that 'assigns atonement' to hand-laying actually teaches you're spiritually docked for skipping it - but the offering is still valid.

argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Yosef
argumentFlow.text: Semikha is a practical difference: R. Yochanan holds that failing to perform semikha at the inauguration invalidates; R. Chanina holds it does not, because semikha does not invalidate ongoing service.

sourceRefs.note: Rav Yosef names semikha as the first practical difference

argumentFlow.label: Semikha does not invalidate ongoing service: baraita from Lev. 1:4
argumentFlow.speaker: Tanna (baraita)
argumentFlow.text: Lev. 1:4 says 'he shall lay his hand and it shall be accepted for him to atone.' Does hand-laying atone? Only blood atones (Lev. 17:11)! So 'to atone' here means: if you treat semikha as optional, the Torah credits you as if you did not achieve ideal atonement - even though you did atone.

sourceRefs.note: The baraita's own question, 'does semikha atone?'
Baraita proving semikha is a shirei mitzva, not an invalidation condition

argumentFlow.label: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: tenufah diverges
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
argumentFlow.text: Tenufah (waving) is another practical difference, following the same structure: 'to wave it to make atonement' - but waving does not atone. It is a shirei mitzva. Therefore R. Chanina holds omitting it does not invalidate the inauguration.

sourceRefs.note: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak names tenufah as the second difference

argumentFlow.label: Tenufah proof: same baraita structure
argumentFlow.speaker: Tanna (baraita)
argumentFlow.text: The tenufah verse says 'to wave to atone' - but waving does not atone. Same reasoning as semikha: treating tenufah as optional means the Torah credits you with incomplete atonement, but you still atoned. Tenufah is a shirei mitzva.

sourceRefs.note: Baraita for tenufah parallel to semikha

argumentFlow.label: Rav Pappa: prisha diverges
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Pappa
argumentFlow.text: Prisha (sequestering) is a third difference. R. Yochanan holds omitting it invalidates the inauguration; R. Chanina holds it does not, since (per the same test used for semikha and tenufah) it does not invalidate ongoing service. The proof for this follows.

sourceRefs.note: Rav Pappa names prisha as the third difference

argumentFlow.label: Prisha proof: word choice for the backup priest
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Pappa
argumentFlow.text: Rav Pappa asks: for future generations, how do we know sequestering does not invalidate? The proof lies in the mishna's own wording for the backup priest: its language designates him without requiring that he already be kept separate in advance. If sequestering were indispensable, the backup would need advance separation too - the word choice proves it is not. Since sequestering does not invalidate ongoing service, R. Chanina holds it does not invalidate the inauguration either.

sourceRefs.note: Rav Pappa's question introducing the word-choice proof; the proof's own wording completes in the sentence that opens the next sugya's own segment

conceptRefs.label: Shirei Mitzva - residual optional mitzva component
R. Yochanan vs. R. Chanina: scope of inauguration requirements

misconceptions.misconception: Shirei mitzva means the act is unimportant or spiritually trivial.
misconceptions.correction: A shirei mitzva is a real mitzva obligation whose omission registers as spiritual incompleteness - the Torah still counts it against you. It differs from an indispensable condition in that its omission does not void the service.

misconceptions.misconception: The verse 'it shall be accepted to atone' proves that hand-laying itself accomplishes atonement.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara reads this verse through the lens of Lev. 17:11, which unambiguously limits atonement to blood. The verse about semikha must therefore be understood as a conditional warning: omitting semikha leaves your atonement spiritually incomplete, even though the blood still atones.

visualizableElements.item: Side-by-side table: three inauguration requirements (semikha, tenufah, prisha) with R. Yochanan's ruling (invalidates) vs. R. Chanina's ruling (does not), each with a one-line proof
Shirei mitzva spectrum diagram: on one end 'core atonement mechanism (blood),' on the other 'totally optional action.' Semikha and tenufah sit in the middle - real but not invalidating.

quizSeeds.question: What is the practical halakhic difference between R. Yochanan and R. Chanina regarding inauguration requirements?
quizSeeds.answer: R. Yochanan: any requirement that was written in the inauguration passage invalidates the service if omitted, even if it would not invalidate ongoing service. R. Chanina: only requirements that would invalidate ordinary ongoing service also invalidate the inauguration.

quizSeeds.question: How does the Gemara explain Lev. 1:4's phrase 'to atone' in connection with semikha, if only blood actually atones?
quizSeeds.answer: The Gemara classifies semikha as a 'shirei mitzva.' When the verse says 'to atone,' it does not mean semikha mechanically causes atonement. Rather, if you treat semikha as optional and skip it, the Torah credits you as if your atonement were incomplete - even though the blood did atone. The phrase is a warning about spiritual incompleteness, not a claim about the mechanism.

quizSeeds.question: How does Rav Pappa prove that prisha does not invalidate ongoing sacrificial service?
quizSeeds.answer: From the mishna's own word choice for the backup priest: its language designates him without requiring he already be kept separate in advance. If sequestering were indispensable, the backup would also need formal advance separation. The mishna's wording proves sequestering is not an invalidation condition.

alternateAngles: The Gemara's shirei mitzva category reveals a theology of mitzva performance: there is a difference between 'you atoned' (valid service, blood accepted) and 'you atoned optimally' (full performance of all mitzva components). The Torah cares about both, even if only the latter is legally indispensable.

display.title: Ravina adds rivui and meshicha; R. Yitzchak bar Bisna gives the source for R. Yochanan's principle
display.oneLine: Ravina adds wearing priestly garments for seven days (rivui shiva) and anointing for seven days (meshicha shiva) to the list of divergences; a baraita proves any combination of these suffices; R. Yitzchak bar Bisna derives R. Yochanan's invalidation principle from 'kachah' - and the daf cuts off mid-thought right after affirming it works for what is explicitly written.
display.shortSummary: Ravina identifies two more practical differences: rivui shiva (wearing the full set of priestly garments across seven days) and meshicha shiva (anointing across seven days). A baraita on Lev. 16:32 ('the priest who shall be anointed and who shall be consecrated') proves that any combination of anointing and garment-wearing over seven days suffices. The need for anointing over seven days is derived from a juxtaposition: since garment-wearing requires seven days, and anointing is juxtaposed to garment-wearing, anointing also requires seven days. R. Yitzchak bar Bisna then gives the source for R. Yochanan's broad invalidation principle: the word 'kachah' (thus/so) in 'do thus to Aaron and his sons' means exact replication is required, making all explicitly written inauguration details indispensable. The daf affirms this works for what is explicitly stated ('tinach kol milta') and then cuts off mid-sentence, ending on the single dangling word 'milta.'
display.whats: Ravina adds two more items to the list: rivui shiva (the Kohen Gadol wearing the full priestly garments on each of the seven days) and meshicha shiva (anointing him on each of the seven days). R. Yochanan holds omitting either invalidates; R. Chanina holds neither does, because neither invalidates ongoing service. A baraita on Lev. 16:32 establishes that any combination of anointing and garment-wearing over seven days makes a valid Kohen Gadol: Exod. 29:30 says 'seven days shall the son wear them,' implying that wearing garments for seven days - or anointing for seven days - or both - all suffice. The source that anointing requires seven days ab initio: it is juxtaposed to garment-wearing in a verse ('the sacred garments of Aaron shall be for his sons to be anointed in them and consecrated in them'), and since garment-wearing requires seven days, anointing does too. R. Yitzchak bar Bisna then derives R. Yochanan's principle: the word 'kachah' in 'do thus to Aaron and his sons' means exact replication, so every detail written in the inauguration passage must be observed exactly - and failure to do so invalidates. The Gemara affirms this works well for anything explicitly stated ('tinach kol milta') - and the sentence cuts off there, ending the daf on the single word 'milta.' Per Rashi's own note on this word, the anticipated continuation on the next page asks about requirements written elsewhere in the Torah, though that question is not itself stated within 5a's own text.
display.hint: The word 'kachah' (thus) in a Torah command signals exact replication of what's explicitly written at that point - but the daf's sentence affirming this cuts off mid-thought. What might the missing continuation ask?

Per Rashi's note on this word, the anticipated continuation (on the next page) will ask about requirements written outside the inauguration passage - but that is Rashi's own anticipation, not text stated on this page.

The daf itself stops mid-sentence right after affirming this works - it does not yet raise the further question of requirements written elsewhere, which per Rashi's note is answered only on the next page.

reasoningPattern.notes: The word 'kachah' (thus/so) in a command signals exact replication of whatever is listed at that point in the text. 5a's own text affirms this scope holds ('tinach kol milta') and then cuts off before addressing anything beyond it.

The Gemara begins to affirm that this works for anything explicitly written - and the sentence is cut off there, ending the daf on the single word 'milta.' Rashi's own note reveals what the continuation will ask, but that question is not yet on this page.

Yitzchak bar Bisna finds the source for R. Yochanan's whole position - the word 'kachah' - and the daf cuts off right after affirming it works, on the single dangling word 'milta.'

argumentFlow.label: Ravina: rivui shiva and meshicha shiva diverge
argumentFlow.speaker: Ravina
argumentFlow.text: Two more practical differences: rivui shiva (wearing the full set of priestly garments on each of the seven inauguration days) and meshicha shiva (anointing on each of the seven days). R. Yochanan holds omitting either invalidates; R. Chanina holds neither does, as neither invalidates ongoing service.

sourceRefs.note: Ravina names rivui shiva and meshicha shiva as the fourth and fifth differences

argumentFlow.label: Lev. 16:32: any combination of anointing and garment-wearing over seven days suffices
argumentFlow.speaker: Tanna (baraita)
argumentFlow.text: Lev. 16:32 says 'the priest who shall be anointed and who shall be consecrated.' Since the YK service already requires a Kohen Gadol, why restate it? The verse teaches: from Exod. 29:30 ('seven days shall the son wear them'), I know only that seven-day garment-wearing AND seven-day anointing validates. What about one without the other? The verse covers all cases: any combination is valid.

sourceRefs.note: Derivation working through the combinations of rivui/meshicha

argumentFlow.label: Source for meshicha requiring seven days ab initio
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: From Exodus 29:29: 'The sacred garments of Aaron shall be for his sons to be anointed in them and consecrated in them.' Anointing is juxtaposed to garment-wearing. Just as garment-wearing must be done for seven days ab initio (from Exod. 29:30), so too anointing must be done for seven days ab initio.

sourceRefs.note: Juxtaposition proof: anointing requires seven days like garment-wearing

argumentFlow.speaker: R. Yitzchak bar Bisna
argumentFlow.text: The source for R. Yochanan's position: the word 'kachah' (thus/so) in 'do thus to Aaron and his sons' (Exodus 29:35). 'Kachah' means exact replication - every detail written in the inauguration passage must be observed exactly, and failure to do so invalidates.

sourceRefs.note: R. Yitzchak bar Bisna identifies 'kachah' as R. Yochanan's proof-text

Per Rashi's own note on this line, the anticipated continuation (on the next page) asks where we derive that requirements written elsewhere in the Torah, outside the inauguration passage, also invalidate - but that question is not itself stated within 5a's own text, only anticipated by Rashi.

misconceptions.misconception: For the Kohen Gadol's inauguration to be valid, he must both wear the garments and be anointed on all seven days.
misconceptions.correction: The baraita derives from Lev. 16:32 that any combination of seven days of garment-wearing and seven days of anointing suffices. Even seven days of only one of these without the other is valid. The verse's redundancy teaches 'mikol makom' - validity in any case.

quizSeeds.question: Does the Kohen Gadol need to both wear the priestly garments AND be anointed for all seven inauguration days in order for the inauguration to be valid?
quizSeeds.answer: No. The baraita derived from Lev. 16:32 teaches 'mikol makom' - in any case. If he was anointed for seven days but did not wear the garments for seven days, or wore them for seven days without anointing, the inauguration is still valid. Any combination of the two requirements over seven days suffices.

quizSeeds.question: What is R. Yitzchak bar Bisna's source for R. Yochanan's principle that all inauguration requirements are indispensable?
quizSeeds.answer: The word 'kachah' (thus/so) in 'do thus to Aaron and his sons' (Exodus 29:35). 'Kachah' signals exact replication - every detail written in the inauguration passage must be performed exactly, and failure invalidates the service.

quizSeeds.question: Why does the daf end with an open question?
quizSeeds.answer: The Gemara affirms that 'kachah' works for what is explicitly written in the inauguration passage ('tinach kol milta'), then cuts off mid-thought at the very end of the daf. Rashi's own note on the final word anticipates that the next page will ask about requirements written elsewhere in the Torah (such as the priestly garment details in Exod. 28) - but that question itself is not stated within 5a's own text.

alternateAngles: The 'any combination suffices' ruling is a classic example of the Gemara using a seemingly redundant verse to expand rather than restrict a rule. A verse that appears to require both anointing and garments actually teaches that either alone suffices. Redundancy in the Torah is always information.

glossary.en: Laying hands on an offering. The worshipper (or Kohen) lays both hands on the head of the animal and leans on it with full weight before it is slaughtered. The Gemara establishes that semikha is a 'shirei mitzva' - a real mitzva component whose omission leaves atonement spiritually incomplete, but which does not invalidate the service.

Waving an offering. Certain offerings or their components are waved before God as part of the ritual. Like semikha, tenufah is a shirei mitzva: the verse seems to attribute atonement to it, but only blood actually atones. Omitting it does not invalidate the service.

A residual or secondary mitzva component - one that complements the core act but does not itself accomplish the primary religious function. If omitted, the Torah treats you as having fallen short of ideal performance, even though the core action (and its legal effect) remain valid. Semikha and tenufah are examples.

Wearing the full set of priestly garments across the seven inauguration days / Anointing with the sacred oil across the seven inauguration days. Both are inauguration requirements that do not invalidate ongoing priestly service. R. Yochanan holds omitting either in the inauguration context invalidates; R. Chanina holds neither does. The baraita teaches that any combination of seven days of garment-wearing or anointing is sufficient to validate the inauguration.

rashiTranslations.en: 'Something that does not invalidate for future generations' - the Gemara explains this below. 'A residual mitzvah' -
meaning he was not careful to count it as [part of] the mitzvah and did not lean [on the animal]. 'As if he had not atoned' - in the choicest manner.
'And he shall be atoned' - since atonement is only through blood, as we say in Zevachim (6a): 'he atoned'
refers to the man - meaning the essential atonement is through blood, but he has not atoned
in the choicest manner. 'And it does not teach they separate him' -
even though he was not separated, if a disqualification occurs
with the first [High Priest], this second one serves. From this we learn that
separation does not invalidate the service.
'Seven days of increase' - that the Kohen Gadol serves for seven
consecutive days when he is appointed to the high priesthood
and wears eight garments during
service; 'increase' means multiplication - he multiplies his
garments, since he serves in eight while the ordinary priest
serves in four. 'Seven days of anointing' - [that they place
the anointing oil on his head and between his eyelids] for seven
days consecutively. 'All that is written concerning them' -
'seven days shall he fill' etc. (Leviticus 8:33), and every filling-of-hands
mentioned there refers to the wearing of garments, as it is said
(Exodus 29:29): 'and the sacred garments which are Aaron's
shall be for his sons after him,
to be anointed in them' etc.; and anointing too
requires all seven, since anointing
is juxtaposed to increase. 'And the priest who is anointed'
'in his place' - this is written regarding Yom Kippur, in Acharei Mot.
'What does Scripture teach?' - if it is to teach
that the service must be by the Kohen Gadol, but the entire passage
already speaks of Aaron: 'Aaron shall come,'
'Aaron shall place,' 'Aaron shall offer,'
'and Aaron shall come' (Leviticus 16:3). 'Because it is said' -
in the portion of Tetzaveh: 'seven days
shall the priest who succeeds him from among his sons wear them, who
comes in his place into the high priesthood, who shall enter
on Yom Kippur into the Tent of Meeting
to serve in the sanctuary.' 'I would only know' - that he
is qualified to enter the Tent of Meeting on Yom Kippur
if he had both seven days of increase and seven of anointing when appointed;
and below the Gemara asks
where seven days of anointing is written.
'Even one hour' - we do not read this [variant].

'The matter' - the daf ends mid-word here; Rashi's comment continues on 5b, where the Gemara asks from where we derive that requirements written elsewhere (outside the inauguration passage) also invalidate.
